q: Though all his accomplishments make Ezra Meeker seem larger than life, he was actually how tall?
choices: Well over six feet, like a mountain man
Tall enough to see over oxen without standing on a crate
teach: Ezra was notably short — a 5′1″ fireplug who was still taller than his bride, Eliza Jane, who stood just 4′8″.

q: The Meeker family's original overland emigration to Oregon Territory is associated with which era?
teach: The 1852 overland migration is the chapter that defines the Meekers — the great 'flood' year of Oregon Trail travel.

q: At journey's end, many families faced land policy questions. A common tension was:
choices: Donation land claims vs later fees and filings as territories matured
Land was assigned by dice at The Dalles
Free land with no paperwork anywhere
teach: Oregon's donation land era and later Washington filings are both part of how Ezra's generation actually secured farms.

q: How old would a pioneer need to be to file for a donation land claim?
teach: Claimants had to be at least 21 — the age of majority in the 1850s — before they could file.

q: What major river did pioneers need to cross to proceed along the Oregon Trail?
teach: The Sweetwater, with its granite and diorite reaches, was a defining crossing — and the river where Ezra's youngest brother drowned.

q: How might a pioneer have crossed a river along the Oregon Trail?
teach: Typically pioneers could ford the river and risk losing life, livestock, and cargo; pay a large fee for a ferry; or caulk their wagons and float them across.

q: What is the role of a wagon master?
choices: A professional gambler and card shark
Guide pioneers over the correct trails
teach: A wagon master knew the route — ground speed, river crossings, camps — and guided the company safely over the correct trails.

q: What year did Washington become a state?
teach: Washington joined the Union on November 11, 1889 — four decades after the Meekers crossed the plains.

q: When did Washington become a territory?
teach: Congress carved Washington out of the northern half of Oregon Territory in 1853.

q: True or False: Washington was once a part of the Oregon Territory.
teach: What is now Washington State was once a part of the Oregon Territory.

q: Where did Ezra and Eliza Jane Meeker land after their journey on the Oregon Trail?
teach: Eliza Jane was so sick on arrival that she had to be carried from the ferry to their lodgings. The Meekers didn't stay long — there was little work and few places to live.

q: How many family members did Ezra Meeker lose on the Oregon Trail?
teach: Ezra lost his mother Phoebe, who died of cholera, and his youngest brother Usual, who drowned in the Sweetwater River.

q: What year did Phoebe Meeker, Ezra Meeker's mother, die on the Oregon Trail?
teach: Phoebe Meeker died just outside Fort Laramie after contracting cholera.

q: Where did Ezra Meeker's Oregon Trail trip begin?
teach: The Meekers rolled out of Eddyville, Iowa, in 1852.

q: On the 1852 trail, Ezra and Eliza Jane's baby Marion was:
choices: Seven weeks old when they left Iowa
teach: Marion Jasper Meeker was just seven weeks old when the wagons rolled — Eliza McAuley's diary calls him 'Dickie.'

q: When the Meekers reached Portland in October 1852, they had:
teach: Nearly broke after the trail — Ezra worked the Mary Melville wharf for $40 while his brother Oliver ran a boarding house.

q: Ezra Meeker began his famous Oregon Trail Monument Expedition at about age:
teach: At 76 he launched the Monument Expedition (1906–1908) — and went on to travel the trail by wagon, automobile, and airplane.

q: True or False: Horses were the most cost-effective animal to pull covered wagons.
teach: Oxen were the workhorses — hardier, able to pull more weight, less likely to be stolen, and able to pull loads for longer stretches.

q: In what year did the remaining members of Ezra Meeker's family travel over the Oregon Trail?
teach: The rest of the family crossed in 1854, two years after Ezra made the trip.

q: Ezra Meeker first saw what is now present-day Puyallup in:
teach: Scouting Puget Sound in 1853, brothers Ezra and Oliver entered the Puyallup River — the huge trees discouraged them then.

q: In order to bring the rest of his family west, Ezra Meeker:
choices: Sent his brother Oliver back over the trail to guide them
Built each of his siblings their own cabin
Wrote and told them not to come
teach: Ezra sent Oliver back over the trail to guide the rest of the family west.

q: Ezra donated his 1906 covered wagon to the Washington State Historical Society in:
choices: 1919 — with tens of thousands of pages of papers
teach: January 1919 — the wagon, taxidermy oxen, and roughly 50,000 pages of letters; rediscovered in 1953 in a glass case.

q: Which branch of the Oregon Trail did Ezra Meeker's family travel on when joining him in the west?
teach: The family came in over the Naches Trail — the only Oregon Trail branch that runs through Washington.

q: In what year did Ezra Meeker first travel the Oregon Trail?
teach: Ezra made his first crossing in 1852 — the peak 'flood' year of overland travel.

q: Only one of Ezra Meeker's full siblings did not travel on the Oregon Trail. Which one was it?
teach: John Valentine Meeker sailed west by steamship instead — his ship wrecked and his family spent days stranded on a deserted island before being rescued and reaching Washington Territory.

q: Why did Ezra Meeker retrace the Oregon Trail in 1906?
choices: To preserve its history and mark the trail
teach: To preserve its history and mark the trail — before its landmarks vanished, Ezra set out to make the route known and remembered.

q: What mode of transportation did Meeker use in his 1916 trail journey?
teach: Ezra Meeker traveled in a 1916 Pathfinder car on loan from the Pathfinder company.

q: True or False: The family of Martin Ballard traveled on the Oregon Trail with the Meekers in 1852.
teach: The Ballard family would reunite with the Meekers 40 years later at a dinner held at the Meeker Mansion.

q: How many people are thought to have died on the Oregon Trail?
teach: Historians estimate 20,000 to 30,000 people likely died along the trail. Many graves went unmarked, had markers moved, or were marked with biodegradable wood — making exact numbers hard to pin down.

q: What was a realistic daily water requirement for one ox on a hot trail day?
teach: A working ox drinks plenty — roughly 8–10 gallons on a hot day, and watering stops drove the whole daily travel schedule.

q: Which disease terrorized wagon trains in many trail-era diaries?
teach: Dysentery — and fellow water-borne ills like cholera — filled trail diaries and graves.

q: Which Wyoming landmark did emigrants strive to reach 'by the Fourth'?
teach: Independence Rock was the trail's great milestone — parties pushed hard to reach it by the Fourth of July.

q: True or False: Pioneers typically rode all the way to Oregon in their wagons.
teach: Wagons were packed with most families' possessions and had no springs, so pioneers of all ages typically walked alongside or behind them.

q: True or False: In hot, dry climates, pioneer women would take off their heavy dresses and wear only their underclothes on the trail.
teach: A few small groups of ladies experimented with bloomer-style puffy pants, but most pioneer women wore lighter cotton or calico travel dresses with shorter hems.

q: True or False: Pioneers burned buffalo chips along the trail to keep warm and to cook meals.
teach: With resources scarce and meals to cook, pioneers made do with what was on hand — dried buffalo dung burned well.

q: What is the name of the first wagon party to cross the Naches Trail?
teach: The Longmire-Biles Party was the first to bring wagons over the Naches route.

q: Covered wagons typically travel how fast?
teach: A loaded wagon crept along at about 2 miles per hour — a walking pace, mile after mile.

q: What stunt made headlines on Meeker's 1920s Oregon Trail expedition?
choices: Flying part of the route by airplane in his nineties
teach: One of Meeker's favorite ways to travel — the 1924 trip took 23 hours at around 100 mph with five stops, a journey his wagon had made in five months at 2 mph.

q: True or False: Axles on wagons broke more often than Native raids on wagon parties.
teach: Despite the movies, attacks on wagon parties by Native Americans were the exception rather than the rule — broken axles were far more common.

q: True or False: Oregon Trail guidebooks were the best way to navigate the trail.
teach: Guidebooks were often wildly inaccurate — outdated information, occasionally dangerous advice, and some written with no knowledge of the actual trail, often as pure marketing devices.

q: Who was the most famous Oregon Trail pioneer?
teach: For the monument crusade, the retracings, and the newsreel fame, no pioneer is more tied to the trail's memory than Ezra Meeker.

q: In his old age, Meeker lobbied hardest for governments to:
choices: Sell the trail to private mines
Mark the Oregon Trail and build a highway that would stretch from East to West
teach: Meeker's late-life campaign pushed for trail markers and a coast-to-coast highway — memory tourism decades early.

q: True or False: Pioneers left behind guest books.
teach: Pioneers often carved their names and the date they traveled into surrounding rocks — what historians call giant stone guest books.

q: True or False: Conestoga wagons were the wagon of choice for most pioneer families.
teach: Families typically chose the compact Prairie Schooner — it needed fewer oxen and survived rough terrain better. Conestogas were massive merchant wagons.

q: Donation land claims promised 360 acres of free land to single white males and this much land to married couples:
teach: Married couples could claim a full section — 640 acres — while single men received 360. That asymmetry shaped who got land.

q: What was one of the most dangerous natural features pioneers faced on the trail?
choices: Rivers — ferries cost money; fords could drown people, animals, and supplies
teach: River crossings were the great choke point — pay a ferry, or ford and risk drowning people, stock, and cargo. Diaries cluster tragedy at water.

q: The Oregon Trail typically began in which city?
teach: Independence, Missouri, was the great jumping-off point for overland trains.

q: What city was most commonly known as the end of the Oregon Trail?
teach: Oregon City, at the falls of the Willamette, was the trail's traditional end point.

q: What made the California Trail so different from the other branches of the Oregon Trail?
choices: There were very few resupply points
The trail was smoother on this route
This route was only passable during the winter
teach: The California branch cut through drier, emptier country with very few places to restock.

q: The Naches Trail is the only portion of the Oregon Trail to run through which state?
teach: Washington's only stretch of the Oregon Trail is the Naches route over the Cascades.

q: The Applegate Trail was designed to avoid what?
teach: The Applegate cutoff was laid out to dodge the deadly Columbia River passage.

q: The Mormon Trail ended in which western city?
teach: The Mormon Trail ended at Salt Lake City, the heart of pioneer settlement in the Great Basin.

q: Approximately how long was the Oregon Trail?
teach: The main route stretched roughly 2,000 miles from the Missouri to the Willamette Valley.

q: How long did it typically take to travel the Oregon Trail?
teach: Most companies needed four to six months of trail time, setting out in spring and arriving before the snows.

q: What was the nickname for the common canvas-topped wagons on the trail?
teach: From a distance, the white canvas-topped wagons bobbed like sails across the grass — hence 'prairie schooners.'

q: Which year is often called the peak 'flood' year of Oregon Trail travel?
teach: 1852 was the great flood year — more emigrants than any prior season, and the year the Meekers themselves crossed in.

q: Outfitting a family of four for the trail could easily run:
teach: A full outfit — wagon, stock, food, and gear — could cost a farm family $600 to $1,200, a fortune in 1850s dollars.

q: Practical guides warned against loading a wagon beyond roughly:
teach: Around 2,000 pounds total — people included — before axles and oxen gave out.

q: Most companies tried to leave Missouri in:
teach: Spring departures let trains clear the mud and still beat the mountain snows.

q: A typical bulk good a family might bring on the Oregon Trail would be:
teach: Flour — alongside bacon, beans, and coffee — was the backbone of the trail larder.

q: Ezra Meeker is known nationally for:
choices: His work saving the Oregon Trail
teach: Meeker's monument crusade and cross-country retracing made him the public face of his campaign to save the Oregon Trail.

q: Many families, including the Meekers, crossed the Oregon Trail for the promise of:
teach: Free land was the magnet — donation claims and later homestead laws drew hundreds of thousands west, the Meekers included.

q: The Oregon Trail is actually made up of multiple starting points, branching trails, and ending points. When describing the trail, historians compare it to:
choices: A rope that is frayed on both ends
teach: The trail wasn't one road — emigrants began in many towns, split into branches across the West, and finished at many places. A frayed rope, not a thread.

q: Unlike depictions in popular culture, wagons typically did not travel in large groups called:
teach: The Hollywood 'wagon train' is mostly myth — most emigrants moved in small, loose companies, not one giant circled column.

q: Ezra and Eliza Jane Meeker traveled over the Oregon Trail with which member of Ezra's family?
teach: Oliver Meeker crossed with Ezra and Eliza Jane in 1852 — the brothers later filed adjacent claims and sold a wagon-box ferry together.

q: Donation land claims promised 360 acres of free land to single white males and this much land to married couples:
teach: Couples could claim a full section — 640 acres — while single men received 360. That asymmetry is why the era's laws shaped who got land.

q: In what year did Ezra Meeker settle in what is now Puyallup?
teach: After the 1852 trail and Puget Sound stops, Ezra's family settled the Puyallup Valley in 1862 — the hop-farming chapter begins there.

q: How many times did Ezra Meeker travel over the Oregon Trail?
choices: Five — 1852, 1906, 1910, 1916 by auto, and 1924 by airplane
teach: Meeker's tally: 1852 by wagon, 1906 monument expedition, 1910 again by ox team, 1916 by automobile, and 1924 by airplane — five crossings.

q: Ezra Meeker's first trail-marking crusade ended in 1908 at which local historic landmark?
teach: The 1906–08 monument expedition finished back at Meeker Mansion in Puyallup — the house Ezra and Eliza Jane built from his hop fortune.

q: What is the most famous party of pioneers to cross the Oregon Trail?
teach: The Donner Party (1846–47) became the trail's most infamous winter disaster — snowbound in the Sierra, it haunts every popular retelling.

q: The 'Prairie Traveler Handbook for Overland Travel' recommends how many of which animal to pull a fully loaded prairie schooner?
choices: Six oxen no matter the load
teach: The Prairie Traveler's math: roughly two oxen for every 2,000 pounds of load — the standard team-size rule for a loaded wagon.
